equation_title: the paper's equation plus a wave
equation_caption: Both add two peaks to a baseline. Each peak is a generalized Gaussian, with an exponent p that sets how sharp it is and different widths on its left and right. Blue marks what this run's winner adds or does differently: one width per peak skewed by an asymmetry factor, a second peak allowed to sit a little off the opposite direction (δ), and a wave that goes once around the circle. The program also fits a parameter it never uses (edge_boost), which the search charged it for; it is left out of the counts on this page.
equation_html:
Paper's equation (11 parameters): f(θ) = b + A₁ exp[−½ (|θ−φ₁| / σ₁±)p₁] + A₂ exp[−½ (|θ−φ₂| / σ₂±)p₂]
This run's winner (13 parameters): f(θ) = b + A₁ exp[−½ (|d₁| / σ₁ e±a₁)p₁] + A₂ exp[−½ (|d₂| / σ₂ e±a₂)p₂] + m cos(θ − ψ), d₂ = θ − φ − π − δ
caveats: An exponent from the first generation. A fitted exponent appeared in generation 0 and in 441 of 470 candidates; in the paper it took several generations. A leakage check found no sign of recall: asked directly, the model did not know the paper and proposed a plain von Mises curve. Its own notes credit the exponent to the plots, which upstream's prompt asks it to compare for “peak sharpness” (see docs/LEAKAGE.md).
The wave barely matters. Added to the paper's equation it lifts median held-out R² by 0.0001 and helps 54% of neurons, close to a coin flip. A few neurons with a lopsided baseline gain a lot.
An unused parameter. The winner fits edge_boost but never uses it, and never fits wrap_asymmetry. This page counts it as a 13-parameter equation; the search's own score charged it for 14.

A floor on peak sharpness. The winner cannot fit p below 1, and about half the locked-test neurons sit there. The paper's equation, refitted here with its own floor of 0.1, gives a median min(p₁, p₂) of 1.06 against the paper's 1.20.

α does not match the paper's numbers. On the same recording we get α ≈ 2.7 (log fit) or 3.8 (linear fit) for the data, against 4.26, and 3.4 for the paper's equation against 4.34. The paper does not state the fit space, neurons or response scaling, and each moves α by up to 1. What does reproduce: the paper's equation decays more slowly than the double Gaussian (3.4 vs 4.4), and closer to the recording.
Different fitter. Candidates are fitted with bounded Levenberg–Marquardt instead of upstream's Adam; scores agree to within about 0.7%.

differences.summary: A baseline plus two generalized-Gaussian peaks, the second roughly opposite the first. The winner swaps the paper's free left and right widths for one width and a skew per peak, keeps the second peak near the opposite direction, narrows the exponent range, and adds a wave that goes once around the circle.

rows.paper: amplitude A₁ ≥ 0 at the preferred direction φ
amplitude A₂ ≥ 0, centred anywhere: opposite φ, shifted by up to ±180°
rows.winner: held within ±29° of the opposite direction

rows.paper: separate left and right width for each peak (4), each at least 0.01 rad
rows.winner: one width per peak plus a skew factor (left = w·e⁻ᵃ, right = w·eᵃ), so the left/right ratio is at most about 4

rows.paper: one exponent per peak (2), between 0.1 and 10
rows.winner: one exponent per peak, between 1 and 3.2
